episode_thesis: Dunne and Kaastrup-Larsen argue the 2025 trend-following drawdown is statistically normal (Man paper) and not caused by crowding or decay, and that a long-vol plus trend blend may help but pure trend remains preferable to the host. In macro, Dunne argues fiscal deficits have decoupled from the cycle and keep long-term yields under upward pressure, while family-office portfolios look diversified but act like equity beta.

speakers.role: Systematic macro commentator (Archive Capital), regular guest co-host

worldview_premises.premise: Fiscal deficits have structurally decoupled from the business cycle (7-8% of GDP at near full employment) and political appetite for austerity is nil, so supply and term-premium pressure point to higher long-term yields.
worldview_premises.support: Deficit-vs-unemployment chart; Eichengreen's pessimism; UK welfare U-turn; his own piece 'all roads lead to higher yields'.

worldview_premises.premise: Dip-buying sentiment is strong: the 2025 S&P rebound from a 21% drawdown in 57 days came without Fed easing, unlike 1998 and 2020.
A trend drawdown of the current size is statistically normal for a 0.5 Sharpe strategy; narratives about choppy markets are easy to attach and often just randomness.
worldview_premises.support: Man and Capstone paper statistics: ~80% chance of a 20% drawdown over 25 years; SG Trend Index fell >15% over 12m only twice in 25 years; past choppy periods (2011-12, 2016-19) ended.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend performance cannot be forecast from a macro scenario; trends emerge when they emerge.
worldview_premises.support: 2022 looked set for higher macro volatility, but 2023-25 had range-bound bonds and four recession scares.

worldview_premises.premise: Drawdown-based timing of managers loses return, and statistics rarely persuade sceptics: staying invested requires prior conviction.
worldview_premises.support: Man paper analysis; experience with allocators.

worldview_premises.premise: Family-office portfolios look diversified but are mostly equity/growth beta, with little commodity or convexity exposure.
worldview_premises.support: UBS 2025 family office asset-allocation chart (about 4% hedge funds, under 1% commodities).

worldview_premises.premise: Fast trend following decayed since the 70s-80s and pairs trading since the 2000s, while trend following and equity-factor long-short had tough but recoverable drawdowns.
Individual managers have had worse drawdowns than the index, shaping investor perception.

speakers.role: Host (Top Traders Unplugged), hedge fund manager
speakers.speaker_note: Caption 'Neil's Krup Larson'. Per ledger correction he gives the C02 market update. States a preference for pure trend over trend plus long volatility.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend profits are positively skewed: rolling 12m returns above +15% occurred about 59 times vs 2 below -15% in 25 years.
worldview_premises.support: Own glance at the SG Trend Index chart (admits 'never do math live').

worldview_premises.premise: Short track records understate drawdown risk; long ones are more informative (79% vs 21% chance of a two-sigma drawdown over 25 vs 5 years).
Crowding is not a good explanation: CTA share of hedge-fund AUM fell from about 27% to 6% while futures volume rose; losses come from reversals in bonds, currencies and equities at once.
Drawdown size depends on whether interest is included in index returns (75% of managers include it).
Long vol gives first-response protection in sudden crashes and trend second-response in prolonged declines; he is lukewarm and prefers pure trend.
Papers defending trend multiply as performance worsens; a wave of them marks a deep drawdown and weak allocator sentiment.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Speaker of the C02 update initially assigned to Dunne; ledger correction attributes to host; 'trim router' is a caption error for trend barometer.
Index figures were swapped in the caption; corrected values (SG CTA -7.8%, SG Trend -10%).

The interest-in-index exchange (C09) is hard to attribute in the caption: the ledger gives the 75%-include-interest and ex-interest 27-28% drawdown figures to the host, but the surrounding turn could be either speaker; the two disagree about whether the index includes interest.
Host computes '59 times' above +15% live and caveats he should not do math live.
Statistics on 'nearly 80%' and 79% drawdown probabilities relayed from papers without assumptions beyond Sharpe and vol.
Man/Capstone papers' conclusions agree with the speakers' priors; both acknowledge sceptics will not be persuaded.
Dunne's earlier prediction of higher yields is not confirmed by the correction; he acknowledges yields fell about 50bp.
Crowding rebuttal caveat: QIS and in-house trend following are not in CTA volume numbers.
Host's long-vol blend scepticism rests on 2020-22 experience, not tested.
Dollar/BIS claim and FT outflow figure are second-hand.
Statement that fast V recoveries without Fed support are a 'twist to common knowledge' is a one-sample comparison.

forward_looking_inputs: Fiscal deficit and bond supply (bill issuance in autumn), term premium, Fed chair appointment, long-bond outflows, dollar hedging flows; for trend performance, sustained trends in bonds, currencies and equities; horizon from months to years.
reader_inferences: The statistical normality argument is about base rates and does not predict when trends return.
Both speakers prefer statistics over narrative for trend drawdowns yet use narrative for macro views.
